value: One of the main red grapes of the Alentejo, where it is blended with Aragonez and Trincadeira and is also often bottled on its own.
source_notes: WoP Aragonez page: blended with Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet in the Alentejo; WoP Alentejo page lists it among the red varieties; Wine Folly Alentejo guide: thrives there, often made as a single varietal or used in blends; Decanter: Esporão makes a dense single variety Alicante Bouschet

value: In the Alentejo it makes deeply coloured, dense and full bodied reds with firm tannins.
source_notes: Wine Folly Alentejo guide: intense colour and body, full bodied, firm tannins; Decanter: dense Alicante Bouschet tasted at Esporão (one word in an older article)

value: One of the most prized white grapes of the Alentejo, at home above all around Vidigueira, and often blended with Arinto or Roupeiro for freshness.
source_notes: WoP: one of the most prized Alentejo varieties, grown almost only around Vidigueira until recently, often blended with Roupeiro and Arinto for acidity; Wine Folly: especially prominent in Vidigueira, often blended with Arinto or Roupeiro for acidity and structure

value: In the Alentejo heat it makes full bodied, firmly structured whites.
source_notes: WoP: firm, full bodied, well structured wines, well suited to the warm plains; Wine Folly Alentejo guide: fuller bodied whites suited to the hot dry climate; Wine Folly region guide: Antão Vaz fuller in style

value: A staple of Alentejo red blends, usually alongside Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet.
source_notes: WoP: blended with Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet in the Alentejo; Wine Folly Alentejo guide: a staple in Alentejo blends; Wine Folly region guide: Tinto Alentejo blends Aragonês, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet and others

value: A grape from the north that has taken well to the warm Alentejo, where it goes into blends and is also bottled on its own.
source_notes: Wine Folly Alentejo guide: originally from the north, now thriving in the Alentejo; Decanter: more recently introduced and taken well to the warm southern soils, Esporão bottles a single variety Touriga Nacional; WoP: has spread south to the Alentejo

value: One of the traditional red grapes of the Alentejo, whose hot, dry climate suits this rot prone vine; it is mostly blended with Aragonez and Alicante Bouschet.
source_notes: WoP Trincadeira: very sensitive to rot so does better in hot dry places, particularly at home in the Alentejo; Decanter: among the original vines of the region; Wine Folly: especially important in the Alentejo, used in blends with Alicante Bouschet; WoP Aragonez: blended with Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet in the Alentejo

value: In the Alentejo it makes lively reds with bright red fruit, fresh acidity and a peppery, spicy edge.
source_notes: Wine Folly Alentejo guide: red fruit, higher acidity, spicy palate, lively reds; WoP: properly ripened it has vibrant raspberry fruit with peppery, spicy complexity and shines in the Alentejo; Decanter: bright, bouncy, fruity Trincadeira in the Alentejo

value: One of the three main white grapes of the Azores, with Arinto dos Açores and Terrantez do Pico; together they must make up at least 85 percent of a Pico or Biscoitos wine.
source_notes: IVV specifications for DO Pico and DO Biscoitos: Arinto dos Açores, Verdelho and Terrantez do Pico represent at least 85 percent of the blend; WoP Açores: predominant varieties in Biscoitos and Pico are Arinto, Terrantez and Verdelho; Club Oenologique: three main grapes, all white, Arinto dos Açores, Verdelho, Terrantez do Pico (sources disagree on which is most planted, so that is left out)

value: The dominant red grape of Bairrada and the base of its classic reds; picked early, it is also used for sparkling wine.
source_notes: WoP Bairrada: reds dominated by Baga, classic style wines mainly based on it; The Wine Society: region dominated by a single grape, baga, also used as base for sparkling wine; Wine Folly: Tinto Bairrada made from Baga, sparkling made with early picked Baga

value: Young Bairrada Baga is firm, tannic and high in acid, often hard at first, and softens over the years into a perfumed, more elegant wine.
source_notes: WoP: lean, tannic, high acid structure, often astringent young, ages well gaining elegance; The Wine Society: tough and astringent in youth, softens with age becoming perfumed; Wine Folly: dense structure and high acidity, top Baga evolves into refined wines over years

value: A secondary red grape in Bairrada, where Baga dominates.
source_notes: WoP Bairrada: reds dominated by Baga, followed by Alfrocheiro, Tinta Pinheira and Touriga Nacional; IVV DO Bairrada specification lists Touriga Nacional among the permitted grapes; The Wine Society: Bairrada dominated by baga

value: Grown in sand by the Atlantic, it makes tart, sharply acidic whites that are low in alcohol.
source_notes: GuildSomm: wines have high acidity and low alcohol, fruit tart and typically green; Vinography (Alder Yarrow): amazing acidity, tart green fruit, tasting note at 11.5 percent alcohol

value: One of the leading red grapes of the Douro, used both for Port and for the region's dry reds, in blends and on its own.
source_notes: IVDP: stands out among the red grapes of new plantings, used on its own or in blends; WoP Douro: one of five red grapes selected for Port; Wine Folly: a Port grape, and Tinto Douro reds use the same grapes; Decanter: Quinta do Crasto single varietal Touriga Nacional

value: In the Dão it makes serious, structured whites that age well for many years.
source_notes: WoP: restricted very much to the Dão, makes serious, rich, structured wines with extraordinary ageing potential; Wine Folly: exceptional quality, can be aged in oak, cellar 5 to 10 years

value: A main red grape of the Dão, where most Portuguese Jaen grows, used in blends and for soft varietal reds.
source_notes: WoP Jaen: at its best in the Dão and most of it is grown there, makes soft, silky reds; WoP Dão: Jaen stands out among the reds; Wine Folly Mencía: best known in Portugal through the Dão; IVV Dão specification: Jaen on the main list of red grapes

value: In the Dão it is lighter in body than Spanish Mencía, giving soft, perfumed reds.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Portuguese Jaen is typically lighter in body, red fruit and floral notes; WoP: at best highly perfumed, soft, silky reds

value: One of the main red grapes of Dão blends, alongside Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and Jaen.
source_notes: WoP Dão: besides Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Jaen and Tinta Roriz stand out; IVV Dão specification: Aragonês on the main list of red grapes with Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and Jaen; WoP Aragonez: spread rapidly through the Dão, usually blended

value: A key red grape of the Dão, used in red blends and also made on its own.
source_notes: WoP Dão: named first among the important red grapes; Wine Folly Touriga Nacional: featured in single varietal wines and red blends from the Douro and Dão; Wine Folly region guide: lists Dão Touriga Nacional as a wine; IVV Dão specification: on the main red list

value: In Bucelas it makes light, dry and sharply fresh whites when young, which grow fuller, golden and more complex with age.
source_notes: IVV Bucelas specification: very light and acidic when young, fuller with complex aromas and a golden tone when older; Wine Folly: Bucelas light bodied, age worthy, very fine with some years of age; WoP Lisboa: Bucelas Arinto offers freshness and longevity

value: One of the main red grapes of Lisboa, used in blends such as the reds of Alenquer.
source_notes: WoP Lisboa: Castelão among the main red varieties; Wine Folly: Alenquer reds made with Castelão, Alfrocheiro, Aragonês and Touriga Nacional; WoP Castelão: especially popular in Lisboa

value: One of the main white grapes of Lisboa, used for aromatic whites, alone or in blends.
source_notes: WoP Lisboa: among the main white varieties; WoP Fernão Pires: particularly important in Lisboa, aromatic, used alone or blended; Wine Folly: aromatic whites of Óbidos and Lourinhã often feature Fernão Pires

value: One of the main red grapes of Lisboa, often blended with Castelão and Touriga Nacional, as in the reds of Alenquer.
source_notes: WoP Lisboa: Aragonez among the main red varieties; WoP Aragonez: has spread through Lisboa, usually blended; Wine Folly: Alenquer reds made with Castelão, Alfrocheiro, Aragonês and Touriga Nacional; The Wine Society: a Lisboa blend of aragonez and castelão from Torres Vedras

value: One of the main red grapes of Lisboa, found in blends such as the reds of Alenquer.
source_notes: WoP Lisboa: Touriga Nacional among the main red varieties; Wine Folly: Alenquer reds made with Castelão, Alfrocheiro, Aragonês and Touriga Nacional

value: One of the four noble white grapes of Madeira, used for the driest style; a Madeira labelled Sercial is dry.
source_notes: WoP Madeira: four noble grapes Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia, in dry to sweet styles respectively; Wine Folly: Sercial makes the most dry and crisp style; IVV Madeira specification: Sercial is a dry wine; Decanter: one of the four noble varieties

value: As Madeira it is the driest and sharpest style, firm and fresh, with a long dry finish.
source_notes: IVV Madeira specification: dry and fresh taste, firm character, long finish growing with age; Wine Folly: the most dry and crisp style of Madeira

value: The most widely planted grape on Madeira and the base of most of its wine, while the four noble white grapes are the ones most prized for long aged bottles.
source_notes: Decanter: most widely planted is Tinta Negra Mole but the four noble varieties are most prized for ageworthy wines; WoP Madeira: most planted, the bulk of the harvest, adapts to all four sweetness styles; WoP Tinta Negra: the main grape of the island; Wine Folly: Rainwater made mostly with Tinta Negra

value: One of the four noble white grapes of Madeira, used for the medium dry style.
source_notes: WoP Madeira: noble grapes in dry, medium dry, semi sweet and sweet styles respectively; Wine Folly: the middle of the road style; IVV Madeira specification: Verdelho is a medium dry wine; WoP Verdelho: responsible for the tangy, off dry style

value: As Madeira it is medium dry and tangy, fuller than Sercial, with acidity that keeps it fresh and notes of dried fruit and spice.
source_notes: IVV Madeira specification: medium dry, full bodied, balanced acidity, long finish, dried fruit, wood and spice; Wine Folly: bright acidity, spiced flavours, richer body than Sercial; WoP Verdelho: tangy, off dry style

value: The grape of Moscatel de Setúbal, a fortified wine left on its skins for months after fortification; the name needs at least 85 percent of this grape, while blends with 67 to 85 percent are sold simply as Setúbal.
source_notes: IVV Setúbal specification: white DO Setúbal at least 67 percent Moscatel de Setúbal, the name Moscatel de Setúbal only with at least 85 percent, skin maceration authorised; WoP Moscatel: same 85 and 67 percent rule, wine left on skins three months or more after brandy is added; The Buyer: long maceration of at least three months after fortification

value: Long macerated on its skins, it tastes of marmalade and flowers when young, then darkens with age and turns nutty, with walnut notes.
source_notes: WoP Moscatel: marmalade, flowers and grapes when young, darkens to golden or mahogany with fig and walnut; IVV specification: floral and orange when young, dried nuts such as hazelnut, almond and walnut when older; The Buyer: orange peel, marmalade, nutty hints in aged examples

value: Grown in fair amounts in the Tejo, where it is valued for the fresh acidity it brings to whites, often blended with Fernão Pires.
source_notes: CVR Tejo: present in reasonable quantity in the Tejo, its main trait is the quality of its acidity which gives freshness; WoP Arinto: in the Alentejo and Tejo its acidity is most useful; Wine Folly: Tejo white blends with Fernão Pires and Arinto

value: Even in the warm Tejo it keeps a bright acidity, giving lively, refreshing whites.
source_notes: CVR Tejo: quality of acidity gives freshness to the wines; WoP Tejo: the lively Arinto produces some of the most refreshing whites, grapes thrive in the warm climate while retaining high natural acidity

value: The main red grape of the Tejo and part of most of its red blends, often alongside Trincadeira.
source_notes: CVR Tejo: the most representative red grape in the Tejo, in practically all red blends, Trincadeira its ideal partner; WoP Castelão: especially popular in the Tejo; Wine Folly: Tejo red blends with Trincadeira and Castelão; IVV DO Tejo specification: the Bairro is ideal for Castelão and Trincadeira

value: In the Tejo it gives intensely perfumed whites, scented with roses and orange.
source_notes: CVR Tejo: high aromatic intensity recalling roses and oranges; WoP Fernão Pires: scents of roses, oranges and tangerines; WoP Tejo: the aromatic Fernão Pires

value: In the Tejo it is the usual partner of Castelão in red blends, and the hot, dry climate suits this rot prone vine.
source_notes: CVR Tejo: the ideal companion of Castelão, very often blended with it; WoP Trincadeira: sensitive to rot, does better in hot dry places, particularly at home in the Ribatejo and Tejo; IVV DO Tejo specification: the Bairro is ideal for Castelão and Trincadeira

value: Richer and fuller than other Vinho Verde whites, with noticeably more alcohol.
source_notes: WoP Alvarinho: compared to other Vinho Verde it makes richer wines, higher in alcohol; WoP Vinho Verde: Monção e Melgaço produce fuller bodied wines with higher alcohol; IVV specification: minimum 11.5 percent alcohol for wines named Alvarinho against 8 or 9 percent otherwise

value: The most fragrant of the Vinho Verde whites, light in body and low in alcohol, with crisp acidity.
source_notes: The Wine Society: the most fragrant of the grapes used for Vinho Verde, which has lowish alcohol; Wine Folly: light body, high acidity, 10 to 11.5 percent alcohol; WoP: refreshing, well balanced acidity
